definition: Typical contribution level before accounting for responses to other participants' later behavior.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = contributes nothing or almost nothing; 5 = contributes about half the feasible endowment; 10 = contributes all or almost all.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: first-round and early-round contribution shares. Interpretation limit: Control for feasible endowment and defaults; do not infer motive.
literature: Ledyard. 1995. "Public Goods: A Survey of Experimental Research." In The Handbook of Experimental Economics. https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691058979/the-handbook-of-experimental-economics; Fischbacher, Gaechter, and Fehr. 2001. "Are People Conditionally Cooperative? Evidence from a Public Goods Experiment." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9

definition: Willingness to sacrifice own immediate material payoff through contribution when contribution is privately costly. This is a behavioral tradeoff, not a claim that altruism, efficiency, warm glow, or conformity is the cause.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = consistently protects private payoff; 5 = makes moderate costly contributions; 10 = repeatedly makes near-maximal costly contributions.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: contribution share plus payoff rule showing private cost. Interpretation limit: Do not distinguish social motives without direct statements or diagnostic variation.
literature: Ledyard. 1995. "Public Goods: A Survey of Experimental Research." In The Handbook of Experimental Economics. https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691058979/the-handbook-of-experimental-economics; Fischbacher, Gaechter, and Fehr. 2001. "Are People Conditionally Cooperative? Evidence from a Public Goods Experiment." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9; Andreoni. 1990. "Impure Altruism and Donations to Public Goods: A Theory of Warm-Glow Giving." Economic Journal. https://doi.org/10.2307/2234133; Charness and Rabin. 2002. "Understanding Social Preferences with Simple Tests." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355302760193904

definition: Withholding contribution while benefiting from substantial peer contribution, including late or situational exploitation.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = does not withhold when peers contribute; 5 = occasional or moderate withholding; 10 = repeated near-total withholding while peers contribute.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: own contribution conditional on visible peer contributions. Interpretation limit: Low contribution without contributing peers is not by itself opportunism.
literature: Ledyard. 1995. "Public Goods: A Survey of Experimental Research." In The Handbook of Experimental Economics. https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691058979/the-handbook-of-experimental-economics; Fischbacher, Gaechter, and Fehr. 2001. "Are People Conditionally Cooperative? Evidence from a Public Goods Experiment." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9; Andreoni. 1988. "Why Free Ride? Strategies and Learning in Public Goods Experiments." Journal of Public Economics. https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(88)90043-6

definition: Degree to which contribution changes in the same direction as observed peer cooperation or explicit cooperative coordination.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = contribution is unresponsive despite diagnostic peer variation; 5 = partial or inconsistent matching; 10 = strong, repeated peer-contingent matching.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/C. Evidence: lagged own-contribution changes after peer contributions or messages. Interpretation limit: Ceiling or floor behavior may make responsiveness unidentifiable.
literature: Fischbacher, Gaechter, and Fehr. 2001. "Are People Conditionally Cooperative? Evidence from a Public Goods Experiment." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9; Keser and van Winden. 2000. "Conditional Cooperation and Voluntary Contributions to Public Goods." Scandinavian Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9442.00182

definition: Sharply changing contribution levels when peer cooperation crosses a salient level.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = smooth or no threshold-like response; 5 = one plausible threshold switch; 10 = repeated sharp switches around a consistent threshold.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/W. Evidence: nonlinear lagged response to peer contribution levels. Interpretation limit: Do not infer a threshold from one change point.
literature: Fischbacher, Gaechter, and Fehr. 2001. "Are People Conditionally Cooperative? Evidence from a Public Goods Experiment." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9

definition: Within-game variability in contribution after accounting for clear peer-contingent responses.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = nearly constant contribution; 5 = moderate variation; 10 = large and frequent unexplained swings.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: within-player contribution range and round-to-round changes. Interpretation limit: Do not bundle volatility with inattention, experimentation, or learning motive.
literature: Ledyard. 1995. "Public Goods: A Survey of Experimental Research." In The Handbook of Experimental Economics. https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691058979/the-handbook-of-experimental-economics; Chaudhuri. 2011. "Sustaining Cooperation in Laboratory Public Goods Experiments: A Selective Survey of the Literature." Experimental Economics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10683-010-9257-1

definition: Gradual directional change in contribution as rounds and experience accumulate.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = sustained downward trend; 5 = no directional trend; 10 = sustained upward trend.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: contribution slope and persistence of updating. Interpretation limit: Separate monotonic trend from event-driven reactions and endgame-only change.
literature: Andreoni. 1988. "Why Free Ride? Strategies and Learning in Public Goods Experiments." Journal of Public Economics. https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(88)90043-6; Chaudhuri. 2011. "Sustaining Cooperation in Laboratory Public Goods Experiments: A Selective Survey of the Literature." Experimental Economics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10683-010-9257-1

definition: Reduction in subsequent contribution after peer free riding, conflict, or another clearly adverse social event.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = maintains or raises contribution after adverse events; 5 = modest or inconsistent withdrawal; 10 = large, repeated withdrawal.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: contribution change after identified adverse peer events. Interpretation limit: Do not combine this score with punishment use or infer negative reciprocity from low payoff alone.
literature: Fischbacher, Gaechter, and Fehr. 2001. "Are People Conditionally Cooperative? Evidence from a Public Goods Experiment." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9; Keser and van Winden. 2000. "Conditional Cooperation and Voluntary Contributions to Public Goods." Scandinavian Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9442.00182; Falk et al. 2018. "Global Evidence on Economic Preferences." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy013

definition: Restoration of contribution after peers resume cooperation or repair a negative interaction.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = does not recover despite clear peer improvement; 5 = partial recovery; 10 = rapid and sustained restoration.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: contribution rebound after an earlier adverse event and later peer improvement. Interpretation limit: Requires both a prior decline and a visible recovery opportunity.
literature: Keser and van Winden. 2000. "Conditional Cooperation and Voluntary Contributions to Public Goods." Scandinavian Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9442.00182; Falk et al. 2018. "Global Evidence on Economic Preferences." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy013

definition: Direction of contribution change near the known or reasonably anticipated end of the game.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = marked endgame decline; 5 = stable late behavior; 10 = marked endgame increase.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: H/D. Evidence: late-round contribution relative to earlier comparable rounds. Interpretation limit: Do not score if horizon knowledge or comparable late choices are absent.
literature: Andreoni. 1988. "Why Free Ride? Strategies and Learning in Public Goods Experiments." Journal of Public Economics. https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(88)90043-6; Chaudhuri. 2011. "Sustaining Cooperation in Laboratory Public Goods Experiments: A Selective Survey of the Literature." Experimental Economics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10683-010-9257-1

definition: Initial willingness to contribute before observing how much other participants contribute.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = begins with near-zero cooperation; 5 = begins around the midpoint; 10 = begins near full cooperation.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/W. Evidence: first contribution and early cooperative message. Interpretation limit: This is a weak behavioral proxy for trust, not a general trust trait.
literature: Fischbacher, Gaechter, and Fehr. 2001. "Are People Conditionally Cooperative? Evidence from a Public Goods Experiment." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00394-9; Falk et al. 2018. "Global Evidence on Economic Preferences." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy013

definition: Behavioral sensitivity to being disadvantaged by low-contributing or higher-earning peers.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = behavior unchanged by visible disadvantage; 5 = moderate or inconsistent reaction; 10 = strong repeated contribution, sanction, or message response to disadvantage.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D/W. Evidence: response to visible contribution or payoff disadvantage. Interpretation limit: Do not infer concern for unobserved counterpart payoffs or collapse all fairness motives together.
literature: Fehr and Schmidt. 1999. "A Theory of Fairness, Competition, and Cooperation." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355399556151; Bolton and Ockenfels. 2000. "ERC: A Theory of Equity, Reciprocity, and Competition." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.90.1.166; Charness and Rabin. 2002. "Understanding Social Preferences with Simple Tests." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355302760193904

definition: Accuracy and consistency in applying game and payoff rules.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeated choices or statements reveal major misunderstanding; 5 = partial understanding or occasional errors; 10 = consistently rule-coherent behavior and explanations.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/C/W. Evidence: dominated actions, mechanism misuse, questions, and accurate rule statements. Interpretation limit: A surprising preference is not confusion unless rules make the action clearly erroneous.
literature: Houser and Kurzban. 2002. "Revisiting Kindness and Confusion in Public Goods Experiments." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/00028280260344605

definition: Evidence that current actions anticipate later rounds, future reactions, or consequences of the game rules.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = exclusively myopic or explicitly no planning; 5 = occasional forward-looking adjustment; 10 = repeated coherent multi-round planning.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/C/W. Evidence: horizon reasoning, contingent plans, anticipatory mechanism use. Interpretation limit: Do not label ordinary lagged reaction as foresight.
literature: Andreoni. 1988. "Why Free Ride? Strategies and Learning in Public Goods Experiments." Journal of Public Economics. https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(88)90043-6; Chaudhuri. 2011. "Sustaining Cooperation in Laboratory Public Goods Experiments: A Selective Survey of the Literature." Experimental Economics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10683-010-9257-1

definition: Frequency and intensity of punishment when it is available.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeated non-use; 5 = occasional or moderate punishment; 10 = frequent or strong punishment.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: punishment opportunities, targets, and amounts. Interpretation limit: Non-use is a low score only when opportunity is present.
literature: Fehr and Gaechter. 2000. "Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.90.4.980

definition: Degree to which punishment is concentrated on lower contributors rather than applied indiscriminately.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = punishment is unrelated to contribution or targets cooperators; 5 = mixed selectivity; 10 = consistently targets the lowest contributors, with severity tracking shortfall.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: target contribution rank and punishment amount. Interpretation limit: Requires actual punishment choices and visible target behavior.
literature: Fehr and Gaechter. 2000. "Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.90.4.980; Herrmann, Thoeni, and Gaechter. 2008. "Antisocial Punishment Across Societies." Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1153808

definition: Whether punishment is directed toward higher or lower contributors.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = primarily punishes high contributors or cooperators; 5 = mixed punishment choices or choices that do not clearly distinguish punishment of higher from lower contributors; 10 = primarily punishes low contributors or defectors.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: contribution rank of punished targets. Interpretation limit: Direction is observable; deterrence, spite, anger, and norm motive usually are not.
literature: Fehr and Gaechter. 2000. "Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.90.4.980; Herrmann, Thoeni, and Gaechter. 2008. "Antisocial Punishment Across Societies." Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1153808

definition: Direction of the next contribution response after the player is punished.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = contribution falls or retaliatory withdrawal follows; 5 = little or inconsistent change; 10 = contribution rises and remains higher.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: contribution before and after received punishment. Interpretation limit: Requires punishment before a later contribution opportunity; score retaliation separately in evidence.
literature: Fehr and Gaechter. 2000. "Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.90.4.980; Nikiforakis. 2008. "Punishment and Counter-punishment in Public Good Games: Can We Really Govern Ourselves?" Journal of Public Economics. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2007.04.008

definition: Frequency and intensity of costly reward when it is available.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeated non-use; 5 = occasional or moderate reward; 10 = frequent or strong reward.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: reward opportunities, targets, and amounts. Interpretation limit: Non-use is a low score only when opportunity is present.
literature: Andreoni, Harbaugh, and Vesterlund. 2003. "The Carrot or the Stick: Rewards, Punishments, and Cooperation." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/000282803322157142; Sefton, Shupp, and Walker. 2007. "The Effect of Rewards and Sanctions in Provision of Public Goods." Economic Inquiry. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1465-7295.2007.00051.x

definition: Degree to which reward is concentrated on higher contributors.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = reward is unrelated to contribution or favors low contributors; 5 = mixed selectivity; 10 = consistently rewards the highest contributors, with amount tracking contribution.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: target contribution rank and reward amount. Interpretation limit: Gratitude or alliance motive needs additional evidence.
literature: Andreoni, Harbaugh, and Vesterlund. 2003. "The Carrot or the Stick: Rewards, Punishments, and Cooperation." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/000282803322157142; Sefton, Shupp, and Walker. 2007. "The Effect of Rewards and Sanctions in Provision of Public Goods." Economic Inquiry. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1465-7295.2007.00051.x

definition: Use of reward conditional on a specific partner's prior favorable treatment or reciprocal interaction.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = rewards show no partner conditioning; 5 = occasional partner-contingent reward; 10 = strong repeated reciprocal reward with the same partner.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D/W. Evidence: partner-specific sequence of received and sent rewards or cooperation. Interpretation limit: Repeatedly rewarding high contributors alone belongs in P20, not P21.
literature: Andreoni, Harbaugh, and Vesterlund. 2003. "The Carrot or the Stick: Rewards, Punishments, and Cooperation." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/000282803322157142; Charness and Rabin. 2002. "Understanding Social Preferences with Simple Tests." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355302760193904

definition: Direction of the next contribution response after the player receives reward.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = contribution falls; 5 = little or inconsistent change; 10 = contribution rises and remains higher.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: contribution before and after received reward. Interpretation limit: Requires reward before a later contribution opportunity; reciprocal rewarding is P21.
literature: Andreoni, Harbaugh, and Vesterlund. 2003. "The Carrot or the Stick: Rewards, Punishments, and Cooperation." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/000282803322157142; Sefton, Shupp, and Walker. 2007. "The Effect of Rewards and Sanctions in Provision of Public Goods." Economic Inquiry. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1465-7295.2007.00051.x

definition: Frequency of participation when a communication channel is available.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = remains silent across opportunities; 5 = occasional participation; 10 = frequent participation across phases.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/D. Evidence: own message count and timing relative to chat opportunities. Interpretation limit: Message content is scored in P24-P30.
literature: Sally. 1995. "Conversation and Cooperation in Social Dilemmas: A Meta-Analysis of Experiments from 1958 to 1992." Rationality and Society. https://doi.org/10.1177/1043463195007001004; Balliet. 2010. "Communication and Cooperation in Social Dilemmas: A Meta-Analytic Review." Journal of Conflict Resolution. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022002709352443; Bochet, Page, and Putterman. 2006. "Communication and Punishment in Voluntary Contribution Experiments." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2003.06.006

definition: Attempts to initiate, organize, or stabilize a group contribution plan.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = no leadership despite clear chat opportunity; 5 = occasional coordination suggestion; 10 = repeated early, specific, and followed-up coordination attempts.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/D. Evidence: proposed targets, plans, reminders, and follow-up. Interpretation limit: Mere verbosity is not leadership.
literature: Koukoumelis, Levati, and Weisser. 2012. "Leading by Words: A Voluntary Contribution Experiment With One-Way Communication." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2011.11.007; Bochet, Page, and Putterman. 2006. "Communication and Punishment in Voluntary Contribution Experiments." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2003.06.006

definition: Making or eliciting explicit nonbinding promises about future contribution.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = avoids commitments despite a diagnostic request or opportunity; 5 = vague or one-off pledge; 10 = repeated specific commitments or active elicitation.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/D. Evidence: explicit pledges, promises, and requests for commitment. Interpretation limit: Separate making a promise from honoring it; consistency informs P30.
literature: Kerr and Kaufman-Gilliland. 1994. "Communication, Commitment, and Cooperation in Social Dilemmas." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.66.3.513; Koessler, Page, and Dulleck. 2021. "Public Cooperation Statements." Journal of Economic Interaction and Coordination. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11403-021-00327-4

definition: Invoking fairness, duty, reciprocity, or a cooperation norm to influence the group.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = no norm appeal despite relevant discussion; 5 = occasional or generic appeal; 10 = repeated specific norm-based persuasion.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/D. Evidence: fairness, duty, reciprocity, or shared-obligation language. Interpretation limit: Pure payoff calculation or neutral coordination belongs in P24 or P14.
literature: Haruvy, Li, McCabe, and Twieg. 2017. "Communication and Visibility in Public Goods Provision." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geb.2017.08.002; Bochet, Page, and Putterman. 2006. "Communication and Punishment in Voluntary Contribution Experiments." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2003.06.006

definition: Directly responding to others while maintaining a supportive, appreciative, or rapport-building tone.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = ignores direct messages or is consistently dismissive; 5 = intermittent neutral responsiveness; 10 = prompt, repeated, supportive engagement.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/D. Evidence: replies, acknowledgments, thanks, encouragement. Interpretation limit: Do not infer agreeableness outside the observed game.
literature: Haruvy, Li, McCabe, and Twieg. 2017. "Communication and Visibility in Public Goods Provision." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geb.2017.08.002; Balliet. 2010. "Communication and Cooperation in Social Dilemmas: A Meta-Analytic Review." Journal of Conflict Resolution. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022002709352443

definition: Use of accusation, shaming, hostility, or escalating interpersonal conflict.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = consistently non-accusatory during conflict opportunities; 5 = occasional mild blame; 10 = repeated strong blame or escalation.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/D. Evidence: accusations, insults, threats, and hostile exchanges. Interpretation limit: Criticism of behavior is not automatically interpersonal escalation.
literature: Haruvy, Li, McCabe, and Twieg. 2017. "Communication and Visibility in Public Goods Provision." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geb.2017.08.002; Bochet, Page, and Putterman. 2006. "Communication and Punishment in Voluntary Contribution Experiments." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2003.06.006

definition: Apologizing, acknowledging error, conceding, or attempting to restore cooperation after a rupture.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = rejects or ignores a clear repair opportunity; 5 = limited or ambiguous repair; 10 = explicit, substantive, and followed-through repair.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/O/D. Evidence: apology, acknowledgment, concession, and subsequent action. Interpretation limit: Use N/A if no rupture or repair opportunity occurred.
literature: Bottom, Gibson, Daniels, and Murnighan. 2002. "When Talk Is Not Cheap: Substantive Penance and Expressions of Intent in Rebuilding Cooperation." Organization Science. https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.13.5.497.7816

definition: Degree to which claims, promises, or strategic messages conflict with later observable action.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = messages and subsequent actions are consistently aligned; 5 = occasional or ambiguous mismatch; 10 = repeated clear contradictions or false promises.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: C/O/D/W. Evidence: promise-action and factual-claim-action comparisons. Interpretation limit: Score observable inconsistency; intentional deception requires stronger evidence than mismatch alone.
literature: Kerr and Kaufman-Gilliland. 1994. "Communication, Commitment, and Cooperation in Social Dilemmas." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.66.3.513; Koessler, Page, and Dulleck. 2021. "Public Cooperation Statements." Journal of Economic Interaction and Coordination. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11403-021-00327-4; Bottom, Gibson, Daniels, and Murnighan. 2002. "When Talk Is Not Cheap: Substantive Penance and Expressions of Intent in Rebuilding Cooperation." Organization Science. https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.13.5.497.7816

definition: Consistency with which choices protect or increase the participant's payoff, calculated using their assigned private chip values.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeatedly sacrifices own surplus without an evident strategic reason; 5 = balances own surplus with other considerations; 10 = consistently protects and increases own surplus.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: own surplus of proposals and received offers, realized own payoff changes. Interpretation limit: Do not infer selfish motive from payoff-consistent behavior alone.
literature: Nash. 1950. "The Bargaining Problem." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1907266; Murphy, Ackermann, and Handgraaf. 2011. "Measuring Social Value Orientation." Judgment and Decision Making. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500004204

definition: Tendency to construct or support packages that plausibly create gains for both sides using participant-visible evidence.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeatedly proposes or chooses one-sided or value-destroying terms; 5 = occasional mutually acceptable search; 10 = repeatedly finds accepted, own-profitable packages and adapts to make gains feasible for others.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/W. Evidence: own-positive accepted trades, counterpart acceptance, adaptations that preserve own gain while improving acceptability. Interpretation limit: This is not ex-post joint surplus: counterpart realized private values are hidden in the primary prompt.
literature: Nash. 1950. "The Bargaining Problem." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1907266; Charness and Rabin. 2002. "Understanding Social Preferences with Simple Tests." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355302760193904; Chakraborty and Harbaugh. 2003. "Cheap Talk Comparisons in Multi-Issue Bargaining." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(02)00255-0

definition: Preference for equal or nearly equal quantities of chips on both sides of an exchange, regardless of private chip values.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = routinely uses highly unequal visible quantities; 5 = mixed package forms; 10 = consistently uses equal or near-equal quantities.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/W. Evidence: offered and accepted quantity ratios. Interpretation limit: Equality of quantities is not equality of surplus and does not by itself prove fairness motive.
literature: Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Kagel, Kim, and Moser. 1996. "Fairness in Ultimatum Games with Asymmetric Information and Asymmetric Payoffs." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0026; Fehr and Schmidt. 1999. "A Theory of Fairness, Competition, and Cooperation." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355399556151

definition: Concern with avoiding disadvantage or seeking an advantage relative to others, beyond absolute own surplus.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = accepts own gains without visible rank concern; 5 = ambiguous or occasional concern; 10 = repeatedly sacrifices own gain to avoid visible disadvantage or explicitly seeks relative advantage.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/S/W. Evidence: participant-visible comparative outcomes or explicit optional survey statements plus consistent choices. Interpretation limit: Usually N/A when counterpart payoffs are hidden and no direct statement distinguishes relative concern.
literature: Fehr and Schmidt. 1999. "A Theory of Fairness, Competition, and Cooperation." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355399556151; Bolton and Ockenfels. 2000. "ERC: A Theory of Equity, Reciprocity, and Competition." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.90.1.166; Straub and Murnighan. 1995. "An Experimental Investigation of Ultimatum Games: Information, Fairness, Expectations, and Lowest Acceptable Offers." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(94)00072-M

definition: How much the participant seeks to gain from proposed trades, given the available chips.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = offers terms with little or negative gain for the participant; 5 = a moderate positive gain for the participant; 10 = repeatedly proposes terms giving the participant very large gains.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: the participant's net gain if the offer is accepted, comparing the private value of chips requested and offered. Interpretation limit: Account for the available chips and opportunities to propose or respond.
literature: Nash. 1950. "The Bargaining Problem." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1907266; Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Roth, Prasnikar, Okuno-Fujiwara, and Zamir. 1991. "Bargaining and Market Behavior in Jerusalem, Ljubljana, Pittsburgh, and Tokyo: An Experimental Study." American Economic Review. https://stanford.edu/~alroth/papers/1991_AER_Bargaining_and_Market_Behavior.pdf

definition: Degree to which proposals become more likely to be accepted after observed responder feedback.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeats rejected terms or becomes less acceptable; 5 = inconsistent or modest calibration; 10 = systematically revises terms after feedback and achieves acceptance.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: proposal changes after acceptances and rejections, later acceptance outcomes. Interpretation limit: One accepted offer without prior feedback does not establish adaptation.
literature: Rubinstein. 1982. "Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912531; Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Straub and Murnighan. 1995. "An Experimental Investigation of Ultimatum Games: Information, Fairness, Expectations, and Lowest Acceptable Offers." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(94)00072-M

definition: Preference for exchanging larger multi-chip packages rather than small packages, given the available chips.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = almost exclusively minimum-size exchanges; 5 = mixed package sizes; 10 = repeatedly proposes or accepts broad multi-chip packages.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: total units offered and requested, accepted package size. Interpretation limit: This is an observable preference for package size, not a literature-defined personality trait.
literature: Chakraborty and Harbaugh. 2003. "Cheap Talk Comparisons in Multi-Issue Bargaining." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(02)00255-0

definition: Preference for simple equal-count or low-complexity exchange ratios.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeatedly uses complex or strongly unequal ratios; 5 = mixed complexity; 10 = consistently uses simple one-for-one or equal-count ratios.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: proposal quantity ratios. Interpretation limit: Do not infer fairness or low cognitive ability from simple ratios alone.
literature: Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Chakraborty and Harbaugh. 2003. "Cheap Talk Comparisons in Multi-Issue Bargaining." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(02)00255-0

definition: Use of current holdings in ways that preserve or create later bargaining opportunities.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeatedly exhausts useful inventory or ignores foreseeable constraints; 5 = occasional inventory-aware choices; 10 = coherent multi-turn acquisition, preservation, and later use of chips.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/W. Evidence: sequence of holdings, feasible future offers, later use of acquired chips. Interpretation limit: Requires an interpretable multi-turn sequence; do not infer hidden plans from one trade.
literature: Rubinstein. 1982. "Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912531; Chakraborty and Harbaugh. 2003. "Cheap Talk Comparisons in Multi-Issue Bargaining." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(02)00255-0

definition: Minimum gain the participant requires to accept an offer.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = accepts zero, negative, or very small own-surplus offers; 5 = accepts moderate own gains but rejects poor terms; 10 = accepts only strongly profitable terms.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/O. Evidence: acceptance and rejection decisions in relation to the participant's potential gain. Interpretation limit: Negative-offer rejection alone gives little resolution among moderate and high thresholds.
literature: Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Straub and Murnighan. 1995. "An Experimental Investigation of Ultimatum Games: Information, Fairness, Expectations, and Lowest Acceptable Offers." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(94)00072-M; Roth, Prasnikar, Okuno-Fujiwara, and Zamir. 1991. "Bargaining and Market Behavior in Jerusalem, Ljubljana, Pittsburgh, and Tokyo: An Experimental Study." American Economic Review. https://stanford.edu/~alroth/papers/1991_AER_Bargaining_and_Market_Behavior.pdf

definition: Reliability of accepting offers that clearly increase the participant's payoff under their private chip values.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeatedly declines clearly profitable offers or accepts losses; 5 = inconsistent uptake; 10 = reliably accepts profitable and rejects unprofitable offers.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/O. Evidence: the participant's potential gain and response for each received offer. Interpretation limit: Low uptake can reflect threshold, fairness, signaling, or confusion; note ambiguity rather than assigning motive.
literature: Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Kagel, Kim, and Moser. 1996. "Fairness in Ultimatum Games with Asymmetric Information and Asymmetric Payoffs." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0026

definition: Rejection attributable to visible unfairness or exploitation even when the participant would gain.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = accepts profitable visibly lopsided offers without fairness objection; 5 = inconsistent or ambiguous fairness response; 10 = repeatedly rejects profitable visibly lopsided terms with direct fairness evidence.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/S/W. Evidence: profitable lopsided offers declined plus explicit fairness statement or repeated diagnostic pattern. Interpretation limit: Do not use other participants' private chip values revealed after play; omit the feature when the evidence cannot distinguish motives.
literature: Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Straub and Murnighan. 1995. "An Experimental Investigation of Ultimatum Games: Information, Fairness, Expectations, and Lowest Acceptable Offers." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(94)00072-M; Kagel, Kim, and Moser. 1996. "Fairness in Ultimatum Games with Asymmetric Information and Asymmetric Payoffs." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0026; Fehr and Schmidt. 1999. "A Theory of Fairness, Competition, and Cooperation." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355399556151

definition: Rejecting currently acceptable terms to seek better later terms, conceal information, or discipline proposers.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = takes acceptable gains immediately; 5 = occasional delay with ambiguous purpose; 10 = repeated profitable rejection followed by coherent pursuit of better terms.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D/W. Evidence: profitable rejections, subsequent proposal or response path, optional strategy statement. Interpretation limit: A profitable rejection alone does not reveal signaling or delay strategy.
literature: Rubinstein. 1982. "Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912531; Straub and Murnighan. 1995. "An Experimental Investigation of Ultimatum Games: Information, Fairness, Expectations, and Lowest Acceptable Offers." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(94)00072-M

definition: Revising offers or responses as observed proposals, acceptances, rejections, and changes in chip holdings reveal information about other participants' private chip values.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = ignores repeated diagnostic feedback; 5 = partial or inconsistent updating; 10 = repeated directionally coherent adaptation to revealed preferences.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D/W. Evidence: changes linked to specific observable counterpart choices. Interpretation limit: Do not judge beliefs against counterpart values the participant could not observe.
literature: Kagel, Kim, and Moser. 1996. "Fairness in Ultimatum Games with Asymmetric Information and Asymmetric Payoffs." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0026; Chakraborty and Harbaugh. 2003. "Cheap Talk Comparisons in Multi-Issue Bargaining." Economics Letters. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(02)00255-0

definition: Adjusting later behavior according to which bargaining partner previously accepted, rejected, proposed favorable terms, or held relevant chips.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = no counterparty differentiation despite diagnostic histories; 5 = occasional differentiation; 10 = strong repeated partner-specific adaptation.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D/W. Evidence: earlier interactions with each bargaining partner and subsequent behavior. Interpretation limit: Offers are broadcast to simultaneous responders, so direct targeting is impossible; score only observable conditioning.
literature: Roth, Prasnikar, Okuno-Fujiwara, and Zamir. 1991. "Bargaining and Market Behavior in Jerusalem, Ljubljana, Pittsburgh, and Tokyo: An Experimental Study." American Economic Review. https://stanford.edu/~alroth/papers/1991_AER_Bargaining_and_Market_Behavior.pdf; Kagel, Kim, and Moser. 1996. "Fairness in Ultimatum Games with Asymmetric Information and Asymmetric Payoffs." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0026

definition: Strength of later favorable or unfavorable treatment conditional on a counterpart's prior treatment.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = no relationship conditioning; 5 = occasional reciprocal or retaliatory response; 10 = repeated strong partner-specific reciprocity or retaliation.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D/W. Evidence: favorable or unfavorable prior act followed by partner-specific treatment. Interpretation limit: Record positive versus negative valence in evidence; the scalar measures strength, not valence.
literature: Bolton and Ockenfels. 2000. "ERC: A Theory of Equity, Reciprocity, and Competition." American Economic Review. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.90.1.166; Charness and Rabin. 2002. "Understanding Social Preferences with Simple Tests." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355302760193904; Falk et al. 2018. "Global Evidence on Economic Preferences." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy013

definition: Increase in willingness to trade, compromise, or accept modest gains as opportunities run out.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = becomes less willing or more demanding late; 5 = no systematic late change; 10 = clear late concessions or broader acceptance.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: late versus early claims and acceptance thresholds. Interpretation limit: Requires a known horizon and comparable opportunities.
literature: Rubinstein. 1982. "Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912531

definition: Willingness to risk ending with few or no trades rather than accept modest gains or moderate claims.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = readily compromises or accepts modest positive gains; 5 = balances agreement and claim quality; 10 = persists with high demands or rejections despite repeated breakdown risk.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D/W. Evidence: repeated rejections, rejected proposals, persistent claims, remaining opportunities. Interpretation limit: This is task-specific; do not infer general patience or risk preference.
literature: Rubinstein. 1982. "Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912531; Straub and Murnighan. 1995. "An Experimental Investigation of Ultimatum Games: Information, Fairness, Expectations, and Lowest Acceptable Offers." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(94)00072-M; Falk et al. 2018. "Global Evidence on Economic Preferences." Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy013

definition: Accuracy in calculating payoffs using private chip values and checking whether trades are possible with the available chips.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = repeated clearly dominated or payoff-miscalculated choices; 5 = occasional errors or partial consistency; 10 = consistently payoff-coherent choices.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: D. Evidence: own surplus, feasibility, inventory, explicit confusion reported in the participant survey. Interpretation limit: Treat this as a feature assessing accurate use of the payoff rules, not personality; nonstandard preferences are not automatically errors.
literature: Gueth, Schmittberger, and Schwarze. 1982. "An Experimental Analysis of Ultimatum Bargaining." Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(82)90011-7; Kagel, Kim, and Moser. 1996. "Fairness in Ultimatum Games with Asymmetric Information and Asymmetric Payoffs." Games and Economic Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0026

definition: Degree to which offers and responses change coherently following acceptance, rejection, and payoff feedback.
anchors_0_5_10: 0 = no coherent update across repeated feedback; 5 = occasional or noisy updating; 10 = repeated, directionally coherent improvement or strategy change.
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Code: O/D. Evidence: within-game policy changes after feedback. Interpretation limit: High activity or self-reported effort alone is not adaptation.
literature: Erev and Roth. 1998. "Predicting How People Play Games: Reinforcement Learning in Experimental Games with Unique, Mixed Strategy Equilibria." American Economic Review. https://www.jstor.org/stable/117009; Rubinstein. 1982. "Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model." Econometrica. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912531

definition: How strongly an observed request supports successive reasoning about the opponent's response.
anchors_0_5_10: No iterative response to the opponent; an unstrategic/default request / One-step or weakly diagnostic strategic adjustment / A request diagnostic of deeper recursive reasoning under the stated bonus rule
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: A rule in which iterated reasoning implies an ordered ladder or otherwise distinct strategic requests
literature: Arad & Rubinstein (2012); Nagel (1995); Camerer, Ho & Chong (2004)

definition: How strongly an observed request supports a response to uncertainty about the opponent's choice.
anchors_0_5_10: Choice treats the opponent as irrelevant or follows a fixed default / Simple point belief or modest hedge / Choice is diagnostic of a strategically guarded response to uncertainty about the opponent
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: The request must distinguish an opponent-contingent hedge/best response from endpoint, payoff, and focal alternatives
literature: Goeree, Louis & Zhang (2018); Arad & Rubinstein (2012)

definition: The extent to which an observed request reflects the material payoff consequences of the stated rule.
anchors_0_5_10: Ignores material payoff differences or the game-specific points schedule / Partly trades base points against bonus prospects / Closely tracks the game-specific payoff consequences and avoids costly, low-return actions
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Choice-level payoff facts such as regret, dominance, base-point sacrifice, or response to the transformed points rule
literature: McKelvey & Palfrey (1995); Manning & Horton (2026)

definition: The extent to which an observed request suggests attraction to the upper endpoint beyond what payoff incentives explain.
anchors_0_5_10: No unexplained attraction to the maximum request / Endpoint pull is plausible but confounded with incentives / Defaults to the upper endpoint even when strategic or payoff considerations point elsewhere
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Upper-endpoint choice or a diagnostically close alternative, interpreted relative to payoff incentives
literature: Arad & Rubinstein (2012)

definition: How precisely an observed request follows a payoff-relevant best response or rule-specific target.
anchors_0_5_10: Choice is a clear arithmetic/optimization error or dominated near-miss / Ambiguous or moderately precise execution / Precisely executes a payoff-relevant best response or rule-specific target
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: A diagnostic payoff comparison, best-response fact, dominance fact, or exact rule target
literature: Goeree, Louis & Zhang (2018); McKelvey & Palfrey (1995)

definition: The extent to which an observed request sacrifices secure base payoff to pursue the contingent bonus.
anchors_0_5_10: Protects secure/base payoff and avoids uncertain bonus pursuit / Balanced trade-off / Sacrifices substantial secure/base payoff to pursue the contingent bonus
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: The bonus must be attainable and the request must reveal a meaningful bonus-versus-base-payoff trade-off
literature: Li & Rong (2018); Manning & Horton (2026)

definition: The consistency of the observed request and associated comprehension checks with the stated rules.
anchors_0_5_10: Response/check evidence is inconsistent with the stated rules / Mixed or weak evidence of understanding / Choice and comprehension checks are jointly coherent with the stated rules
evidence_and_interpretation_rules: Choice coherence plus aggregated comprehension-check performance for the same payoff-design–choice pair
literature: Feature assessing understanding of the game instructions; not a personality construct
